title: 'Myelination: Wrapping the Axon So the Signal Jumps'

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Myelin consists of tightly wrapped layers of glial {{c1::plasma membrane}}.
cards.back: The layers are squeezed until almost no cytoplasm remains between turns.
cards.quote: Myelin is glial plasma membrane, made by oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord and by Schwann cells in peripheral nerve.

cards.front: The short gaps between myelin sheaths where voltage-gated sodium channels are densely packed are the {{c1::nodes of Ranvier}}.
cards.back: Action potentials are regenerated at these gaps.
cards.quote: The axon exploits this by packing its voltage-gated sodium channels into short gaps between sheaths, the nodes of Ranvier.

cards.front: How does compact myelin reduce both delays that slow current spreading along an axon?
cards.back: It lowers membrane capacitance and raises membrane resistance, reducing charging demand and current leakage so the next node reaches threshold sooner.
cards.quote: in an ideal sheath of identical compact membranes, the capacitance of the wall falls, and its resistance rises, by roughly that factor.

cards.front: An internode loses insulation while its next node retains sodium channels. What happens to arrival at that node, and why?
cards.back: Arrival is delayed: more current leaks away or charges the exposed membrane, leaving less to bring the next node to threshold.
cards.quote: Either way, less is left for the next stretch, so it reaches threshold later.

cards.front: The g ratio equals axon diameter divided by {{c1::fiber diameter}}.
cards.back: Fiber diameter includes both axon and myelin.
cards.quote: Myelin work uses two diameters: the axon diameter (the axon alone) and the fiber diameter (axon plus myelin).
cards.section: Two diameters, and the g ratio

cards.front: Why does conduction velocity rise roughly linearly with diameter in large myelinated fibers at fixed g ratio?
cards.back: Wider axons have lower axial resistance while internodal capacitance per length stays similar. Longer internodes cover more distance in about the same crossing time.
cards.quote: The time to cross one internode therefore stays about constant while the distance covered per jump grows, so speed rises in proportion to diameter.
cards.section: Two diameters, and the g ratio

cards.front: A 5 µm axon has g = 0.65. Calculate its fiber diameter and radial sheath thickness, using thickness = (fiber diameter − axon diameter)/2.
cards.back: Fiber diameter = 5/0.65 ≈ 7.69 µm. Sheath thickness = (7.69 − 5)/2 ≈ 1.35 µm.
cards.quote: Myelin work uses two diameters: the axon diameter (the axon alone) and the fiber diameter (axon plus myelin).
cards.section: Two diameters, and the g ratio

cards.front: A large myelinated mammalian fiber is 8 µm across. Using velocity ≈ 6 m/s per µm of fiber diameter, find the travel time over 1.2 m; compare a bare fiber at 1 m/s.
cards.back: Myelinated speed ≈ 6 × 8 = 48 m/s; time ≈ 1.2/48 = 0.025 s = 25 ms. Bare time = 1.2/1 = 1.2 s = 1200 ms.
cards.quote: For large myelinated mammalian fibers (several µm and up), velocity ≈ 6 m/s × fiber diameter in µm
cards.section: Two diameters, and the g ratio

cards.front: At fixed g ratio, why does a larger axon gain a greater multiple of its bare conduction speed when wrapped?
cards.back: The lesson's approximate scaling rules give myelinated speed proportional to axon diameter d, but bare speed proportional to √d. Their ratio therefore grows roughly as d/√d = √d: larger axons gain a greater multiple.
cards.quote: The gain itself grows with the square root of diameter, because one speed rises with d and the other with √d.
cards.section: Two diameters, and the g ratio

cards.front: How many internodes does one oligodendrocyte make compared with one myelinating Schwann cell?
cards.back: An oligodendrocyte makes many, usually on different axons; a myelinating Schwann cell makes one on one axon.
cards.quote: In peripheral nerves, a myelinating Schwann cell makes a single internode on a single axon.

cards.front: Several small peripheral axons held unmyelinated in grooves of one Schwann cell form a {{c1::Remak bundle}}.
cards.quote: Schwann cells that meet small axons do not myelinate; they hold several of them in grooves of their membrane, an arrangement called a Remak bundle.

cards.front: Schwann cells from an unmyelinated nerve form myelin after transfer to a normally myelinated nerve. What determines their changed behavior, and what does this experiment leave unidentified?
cards.back: Their new axons direct the changed behavior, supporting axonal control in peripheral nerve. The graft alone does not identify the molecular signal.
cards.quote: Schwann cells from unmyelinated nerves myelinated the axons they met in their new nerve, and the reverse swap gave the reverse result.

cards.front: The main surface signal that sets whether and how thickly a peripheral axon is myelinated is {{c1::neuregulin-1 type III}}.
cards.back: Its active part stays tethered near the axon membrane, so Schwann cells mainly read it through contact.
cards.quote: The main one turned out to be neuregulin-1 type III, a protein on the axon's surface.

cards.front: How do ErbB3 and ErbB2 complement one another when Schwann cells read neuregulin?
cards.back: ErbB3 binds neuregulin but has a weak kinase; ErbB2 binds no ligand but has a strong kinase. Together they signal.
cards.quote: ErbB3 binds neuregulin but has a weak kinase. ErbB2 binds no ligand but has a strong kinase. Paired, they signal.

cards.front: Peripheral axons retain enough neuregulin-1 type III to be wrapped, but its amount falls. At unchanged axon diameter, what happens to g ratio, and why?
cards.back: The g ratio rises: reduced type III produces a thinner sheath, decreasing total fiber diameter while axon diameter stays fixed.
cards.quote: Below a threshold amount of type III, an axon stays bare. Above it, more type III helps make a thicker sheath.

cards.front: Why is neuregulin-1 type III called instructive for peripheral myelination?
cards.back: In sympathetic-neuron/Schwann-cell cultures, adding extra type III to normally bare axons made Schwann cells myelinate them; changing the signal changed the outcome.
cards.quote: giving extra to axons that would stay bare made Schwann cells myelinate them, so supplying it changes the outcome rather than just allowing it.

cards.front: To test whether Schwann cells use total neuregulin-1 type III as a size cue, compare two peripheral axon diameters with matched type III amounts and intact basal lamina/Gpr126 signaling. What would challenge an amount-only readout?
cards.back: Different sheath responses despite matched amounts would challenge an amount-only readout. The stated rules link dose to wrapping and thickness, but diameter sensing by total amount remains a proposal; a strictly proportional readout is unproven.
cards.quote: No one has shown that Schwann cells measure size this way, or that the readout is strictly proportional.

cards.front: Besides axonal neuregulin-1 type III, which two Schwann-cell inputs are required for peripheral myelination?
cards.back: The Schwann cell must lay down its basal lamina and signal through Gpr126, which raises intracellular cAMP.
cards.why: The basal lamina also restrains wrapping of small axons and tunes neuregulin responses; Gpr126 also participates in axon sorting.
cards.quote: The axon's signal is decisive but not enough on its own. Two other inputs are also required, and they are not mere on-switches.

cards.front: Why does the peripheral neuregulin requirement not transfer unchanged to oligodendrocytes?
cards.back: Mouse CNS myelination persists without neuregulin-1/ErbB signaling, although extra neuronal neuregulin can thicken sheaths. It modulates CNS myelination without being required to initiate it.
cards.quote: So neuregulin-1/ErbB signaling is not needed to start wrapping, and the oligodendrocyte brings much of the program itself.
cards.section: In the brain, the oligodendrocyte brings its own program

cards.front: Oligodendrocytes wrap suitable inert plastic fibers without neurons. Does this support an obligatory axonal instruction to initiate wrapping? What remains unresolved?
cards.back: No. It supports an intrinsic wrapping program. It does not establish which living axons will retain sheaths or how activity biases that choice.
cards.quote: In culture, oligodendrocytes will wrap inert plastic fibers of a suitable diameter.
cards.section: In the brain, the oligodendrocyte brings its own program

cards.front: In a zebrafish larva, an axon's vesicle release is blocked while nearby axons release normally. Predict its success in retaining myelin and explain the comparison.
cards.back: It is wrapped less often and has shorter sheaths. Release biases sheath retention; normal neighbors provide a comparison in shared surroundings, though other axonal differences are not excluded.
cards.quote: Release from the axon, which depends on its activity, is one of the cues that biases the choice.
cards.section: In the brain, the oligodendrocyte brings its own program

cards.front: In the zebrafish larval experiment, how would blocking vesicle release affect the increase in sheath number per oligodendrocyte caused by a convulsant drug?
cards.back: It would prevent the increase: the activity-driven increase in sheath number depends on vesicle release in this experiment.
cards.quote: raising activity with a convulsant drug increased it unless release was blocked.
cards.section: In the brain, the oligodendrocyte brings its own program

cards.front: Oligodendrocytes wrap inert fibers; activity manipulations alter zebrafish sheaths, and mouse premotor stimulation adds oligodendrocytes and thickens myelin. What model fits these results, and can it establish a role in adult human learning?
cards.back: Together these results support an intrinsic glial program adjustable by neuronal activity. Under the stated rules, fish and mouse evidence does not establish how much activity-dependent myelination contributes to learning in adult humans.
cards.quote: increased the division of oligodendrocyte precursor cells and the making of new oligodendrocytes, and thickened myelin within the stimulated circuit.
cards.section: In the brain, the oligodendrocyte brings its own program

cards.front: Which myelin membrane faces form the major dense line, and which protein brings them together in CNS myelin?
cards.back: The cytoplasmic faces of successive turns; myelin basic protein (MBP).
cards.why: Positively charged MBP binds negatively charged lipids in facing cytoplasmic leaflets and pulls them together, squeezing out cytoplasm.
cards.quote: A dark major dense line marks where the cytoplasmic faces of successive turns meet

cards.front: Which proteins hold the outer faces of compact myelin together in the CNS and in peripheral nerve?
cards.back: Proteolipid protein (PLP) in the CNS; protein zero (P0) in peripheral nerve.
cards.quote: Other proteins hold the outer faces: proteolipid protein (PLP) in the central nervous system, and protein zero (P0), an immunoglobulin-like adhesion protein, in peripheral nerve.

cards.front: Why is peripheral myelin less affected than brain myelin in shiverer mice lacking nearly all MBP?
cards.back: Peripheral P0 can also hold cytoplasmic faces together, partly compensating for the missing MBP function.
cards.quote: Peripheral nerve in shiverer is far less affected, because P0 can also hold the cytoplasmic faces together there.

cards.front: A large deletion removes a myelin structural gene and nearby DNA; mutants lack compact CNS myelin and tremble. Design a rescue to test whether loss of that gene explains both defects.
cards.back: Add back only a normal copy of the structural gene, expressed in the relevant glia, while retaining the deletion. Compare rescued mutants with unrescued mutants and normal animals. Restored compaction and stopped tremor support causation for those defects, using the stated gene-rescue rule; they do not establish rescue of every phenotype.
cards.quote: So loss of MBP is enough to explain those defects; other features were not tested.

cards.front: Oligodendrocytes pass energy metabolites toward axons through the monocarboxylate transporter {{c1::MCT1}}.
cards.back: This is support beyond electrical insulation.
cards.quote: Oligodendrocytes pass energy metabolites to the axon through a monocarboxylate transporter, MCT1
cards.section: A second job: feeding the axon

cards.front: What is the proposed lactate route from oligodendrocytes to axonal ATP production?
cards.back: Glial glucose breakdown produces lactate, which travels through non-compact myelin channels, exits via MCT1 and enters the axon through a related transporter for mitochondrial ATP production.
cards.why: This remains a proposal; the share of support provided by lactate and the identity of other transferred substances are still being worked out.
cards.quote: One proposal is that the oligodendrocyte breaks glucose down to lactate and hands the lactate to the axon, whose mitochondria use it to make ATP.
cards.section: A second job: feeding the axon

cards.front: A hypothetical oligodendrocyte mutant retains nearly normal-looking myelin, but its axons progressively degenerate. Which glial function does this implicate, and what does appearance alone fail to establish?
cards.back: It implicates long-term axon support beyond insulation. Nearly normal appearance does not exclude subtle sheath defects or identify which missing support causes degeneration.
cards.quote: The sheath was there; something else the glial cell provides was missing.
cards.section: A second job: feeding the axon

cards.front: Which two benefits to axons are lost when an MS lesion destroys myelin and healthy oligodendrocytes?
cards.back: Saltatory conduction and oligodendrocyte support for axon survival.
cards.quote: Without the sheath, saltatory conduction is lost. Without healthy oligodendrocytes, the axon loses its support.

cards.front: Why can disability in multiple sclerosis keep increasing after treatments quiet relapses?
cards.back: Axons may still degenerate through lost sheath/glial support, persistent CNS inflammation incompletely controlled by treatment, and mitochondrial or energy failure.
cards.quote: Together they help explain why disability can keep growing after relapses have been quieted.

cards.front: An MS lesion is successfully remyelinated. Predict the two kinds of axonal benefit and explain why both matter.
cards.back: Saltatory conduction is restored and axon health is supported. Repair replaces the sheath while restoring glial support; the benefit extends beyond recovering signal speed.
cards.quote: The nervous system tries to remyelinate lesions, and remyelination restores saltatory conduction and helps keep axons healthy.

cards.front: In animal models, how does remyelination proceed, and how do the new sheaths compare with the original ones?
cards.back: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells enter lesions, mature and form new sheaths, typically thinner and with shorter internodes.
cards.quote: In animal models, oligodendrocyte precursor cells move in, mature and make new sheaths, which are typically thinner with shorter internodes.

cards.front: Carbon dating finds old oligodendrocytes in human MS lesions that look remyelinated. What does that suggest about repair, and why should the conclusion stay qualified?
cards.back: Surviving oligodendrocytes may contribute new myelin. Old cells in remyelinated-looking tissue suggest this possibility but do not establish the source of every repaired sheath.
cards.quote: carbon dating of MS tissue found that oligodendrocytes in remyelinated-looking lesions were old cells, so surviving oligodendrocytes may make some of the new myelin.

cards.front: Design a mouse comparison testing whether oligodendrocyte loss can damage axons without mature T or B cells. What would a positive result establish, and what would remain unresolved?
cards.back: In mice lacking mature T and B cells, selectively kill oligodendrocytes in one group and leave them intact in matched controls. Greater axon degeneration after cell loss supports harm without adaptive immunity. Under the stated rules, innate immune effects remain possible, and simultaneous loss of sheath and support prevents separating those causes.
cards.quote: Microglia and other innate immune cells are still present, and dying oligodendrocytes activate them.

cards.front: How would you test whether loss of glial fuel delivery can harm axons while separating it from loss of insulation?
cards.back: Keep oligodendrocytes alive, selectively disrupt their metabolite delivery, verify that sheaths remain intact, and compare axon survival with matched controls. Degeneration despite intact sheaths would support a separate support function. This combines the stated metabolite-transfer and insulation rules; sheath thinning would confound the test.
cards.quote: A sharper test leaves the oligodendrocytes alive, removes one thing they supply, such as the transporter MCT1, checks that the sheath stays intact

cards.front: At fixed total fiber diameter, a model fiber starts near the g ratio giving maximal speed. Would adding more myelin by reducing g necessarily increase speed? Why?
cards.back: No. At fixed total diameter, reducing g shrinks the axon as the sheath thickens; the model has an optimum near g = 0.61. Moving below that optimum need not improve speed.
cards.quote: The optimum also depends on what is held fixed
cards.section: How sharp is the g ratio optimum?

cards.front: Removing calcineurin broadly from neural crest cells suggested a role in myelination, but Schwann-cell-specific removal left myelination near normal. What inference is weakened?
cards.back: That calcineurin is required within Schwann cells themselves for myelination; the broader deletion does not isolate that cell-specific requirement.
cards.quote: When a later study removed it from Schwann cells alone, myelination and Krox20 were close to normal.

cards.front: Oligodendrocytes from different CNS regions make different sheath lengths on inert fibers without axons. Which explanation of sheath length does this challenge?
cards.back: It challenges an exclusively axon-instructed explanation: sheath length is partly a program of the oligodendrocyte itself.
cards.quote: Sheath length, too, is partly the glial cell's own program.
cards.section: Oligodendrocytes remember where they came from
